newsitem.title: FRANCE: Former French PM disapproves handling of Thomson.
newsitem.headline: Former French PM disapproves handling of Thomson.

text.p: Former French prime minister Edouard Balladur said in an interview released on Wednesday that he disapproved of the government's handling of the Thomson SA privatisation but agreed with the choice of buyer.

"It would have been better for the government to first have waited for the advice of the privatisation commission before it let know its preference and its estimate of the price," Balladur told the VSD weekly in an interview to be published on Thursday.

Balladur belongs to the same ruling RPR Gaullist party as his successor Alain Juppe and president Jacques Chirac. He served under Socialist president Francois Mitterand and was a candidate in the presidential elections, losing out to Chirac.

Asked whether he agreed with the government's choice to sell Thomson SA, which has a 58 percent stake in defence group Thomson-CSF and 100 percent of consumer electronics group Thomson Multimedia, to Lagardere Groupe and Daewoo Electronics instead of to rival bidder, Alcatel Alsthom, he said he did.
"Looking at the information that I have, yes. But now I hear people say that the choice is not final," he said.
Balladur said that, "In the case of a company whose role is essential for the defence (of France), it is normal that the state's view prevails."

The French government on October 16 said that after studying bids by Lagardere and Alcatel it planned to sell loss-making Thomson SA to Lagardere for one symbolic franc after an 11 billion franc capital injection.
It made its preference known before the state's privatisation commission, which must establish the value of state assets put up for sale, had started to examine the bids.
Normally, the government informs the seven-member independent commission about its preference but does not make it public.
In the case of Thomson, however, the government decided to publish its decision to avoid insider-dealing or a false market in shares of either Thomson-CSF, Alcatel or Lagardere.
The privatisation commission is expected to render its opinion in early December.
Balladur is the most prominent of parliamentarians belonging to the ruling centre-right majority coalition to voice criticism about the Thomson affair.
The Socialist Party and Communist Party want a commission of inquiry to investigate the decision-making process.

Juppe last week unexpectedly announced that there would be a parliamentary debate, but no vote, on the Thomson sale after the privatisation commission decision. This move was widely seen as a bid to silence criticism from the parliamentary majority.
